problem: VLA navigation models (e.g. NaVILA) hallucinate and drift off the path, but existing deviation detection relies on post-hoc heuristics (collision/stagnation), trained auxiliary critics, or slow external LLM API calls, none of which give cheap high-frequency monitoring.
motivation: Real-time deployment needs a detector that adds no training and negligible compute. Attention heads in LLM/LVLMs specialise, so the authors ask whether a frozen VLA already contains heads whose instruction-to-frame attention tracks navigation progress and breaks down at deviation.
key_idea: Select a few 'Navigation Heads' in a frozen VLA whose instruction-to-frame attention forms a diagonal, deviation-sensitive pattern, and flag path deviation from a spike in their relative attention entropy, then trigger a lightweight RL policy to roll back to the last safe checkpoint.
insight: Deviation is visible in the VLA's internal attention: only 3 of 1024 heads suffice, and increasing K beyond 3 does not help under the FER<10% constraint (K ablation). Compared with kinematic heuristics (stagnation, action failure) that miss over 60% of anomalies, attention entropy gives much higher recall (65.1% vs 38.7% step-level on val-unseen) because it captures semantic misalignment before physical stagnation. The detector costs only ~20 ms and no extra VRAM.
method: Trajectory phase labelling: a state machine with patience p over distance-to-next-waypoint deltas labels steps as Normal or Anomaly (N, A, N→A episodes), giving GT for head selection and evaluation.

Navigation head selection: score each head's instruction-to-frame attention on SPL=1 episodes with I_diag = S_uniform·S_peak·(λS_diag+(1−λ)S_shift), then rank candidates by Cohen's d of S_peak between N and A phases.

Entropy-based detection: mean normalized entropy of top-K heads E_t, relative score R_t = E_t / rolling mean over W steps; an anomaly is registered when R_t>τ for P consecutive steps; (K,W,τ,P) are chosen by a 9,000-config grid sweep on the train split with FER<10%.
Safe checkpoint: during the normal phase, continuously save pose, visual history, entropy buffer and attention state for rollback.

RL low-level policy: PPO in IsaacLab, CNN on a 128x128 ego-motion-compensated decaying costmap plus MLP on the relative goal, outputs (v,ω); 14-term dense reward, curriculum 5→20 m, 4.89M params, 0.2 ms.
Sim-to-real system: ROS 2 on Jetson AGX Orin with VLA at ~0.3 Hz and RL at 10 Hz, Fast-LIVO2 + AprilTag EKF odometry, kinematic action smoother.

setting.backbone: NaVILA (VILA-8B / LLaMA-3 8B, frozen) for detection; separate PPO CNN+MLP policy for control
setting.training_data: Detector is training-free; heads and hyperparameters are chosen on 1,000 R2R-CE train episodes (RxR train for the RxR supplement). RL policy is trained in procedurally generated IsaacLab terrain (2,000 obstacles), with no navigation-dataset data.
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB history (8 frames) + instruction for VLA; LiDAR costmap + relative goal for RL; odometry
setting.action_space: VLA: mid-level text actions (e.g. turn 30°, move 75 cm); RL: continuous velocity (v, ω)
setting.simulator: Habitat VLN-CE (R2R/RxR) for detection; IsaacLab for RL
setting.privileged: GT reference path waypoints are used only offline to label phases for head selection/evaluation; the deployed detector needs none. Rollback uses odometry/localization.

numbers.method: Ours (Hnav K=3 entropy detector on NaVILA)
numbers.extra: Deviation-detection metrics, not navigation SR; heads/hyperparameters from train split; 1,839 episodes

numbers.method: Ours (Hnav K=3 entropy detector on NaVILA)

numbers_note: No navigation SR/SPL is reported; numbers are deviation-detection metrics (EDR, FER, Gap, step-level P/R/F1). The abstract's '44.6% / 11.7%' corresponds to val-seen. The K=3 train-split result is EDR 43.9%, FER 9.6%. The RL policy is evaluated separately (SR 87.3%, CR 10.6%, TR 2.0% in IsaacLab), and real-world results are qualitative only.
results: Three navigation heads ([21,12],[16,1],[14,1]) detect 41.9% of deviated episodes at 9.6% FER on R2R val-unseen (step F1 76.4%). This beats stagnation (Gap 23.7%) and action-failure (Gap −4.8%) heuristics. The overhead is +19.8 ms and 0 MB VRAM. The RL policy reaches 87.3% SR against APF 57.4% in simulation, and the full detect-and-rollback pipeline is shown on a real robot.
limitations: Rollback fixes the physical pose but not the VLA's internal context, so the VLA can repeat the same error; no replanning or re-prompting is implemented.
Detection rate is modest (~42–45% of deviated episodes) and drops on RxR (32.7%); the thresholds are tuned on a FER<10% trade-off.
Real-world evaluation is only qualitative, with no quantitative navigation success or recovery metrics; the detector is validated only on NaVILA.
